relation_context.story_before_this_passage:
During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls how a man trampled a girl, then paid her family £100 with a cheque that proved genuine. Enfield names him Hyde, deformed and detestable, still holding the key. Utterson says he knows the other party’s name. They agree never to speak of it again.

Utterson returns home troubled and studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. He calls it madness and fears disgrace. At Cavendish Square, Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful years ago and has never heard of Hyde. Unable to sleep, Utterson resolves to hunt Hyde. Keeping watch by the by-street door, he accosts a small man with a key, who admits Jekyll is out, gives his Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. At Jekyll’s house, Poole confirms Hyde has a key, comes by the dissecting room, and all servants must obey him. Utterson goes home fearing Jekyll is in deep waters.

After dinner, Utterson stays behind with Dr. Jekyll and raises the will. Jekyll calls Lanyon a hide-bound pedant. When Utterson mentions young Hyde, Jekyll pales and refuses to hear more. Utterson offers confidential help, but Jekyll says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses, yet takes great interest in him. Jekyll asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when he is gone. Utterson promises to bear with Hyde and get his rights.

relation_context.previous_passage_tail: [P1] This last, however, was not so easy of accomplishment; for Mr. Hyde had numbered few familiars—even the master of the servant maid had only seen him twice; his family could nowhere be traced; he had never been photographed; and the few who could describe him differed widely, as common observers will. Only on one point were they agreed; and that was the haunting sense of unexpressed deformity with which the fugitive impressed his beholders.

known_before.bio: Mr. Utterson is a Gaunt Street lawyer, kinsman and friend of Richard Enfield, and friend of Dr. Jekyll and Dr. Lanyon. He is a man of blameless past, troubled by old sins. After Enfield showed him a sinister door and named its user, Utterson studied Jekyll's will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde. He consulted Lanyon, watched the by-street door, and accosted Hyde. Later he stayed after Jekyll's dinner and promised to help Hyde for Jekyll's sake. known_before.bio: Poole is the elderly servant and butler at Dr. Jekyll's house, serving his master Dr. Jekyll and obeying the man in the middle as an obeyed superior. He admitted Utterson to Jekyll's house and told him Jekyll had gone out. He confirmed that Hyde has a key and comes by the dissecting room door, that all servants have orders to obey Hyde, and that Hyde never dines there and mostly uses the laboratory. He now continues in his post, bound by orders to obey Hyde.
